conventional_description: Belching, or burping, is the expulsion of gas from the stomach through the mouth. It is a normal reflex that occurs when swallowed air accumulates or when gas is produced during digestion. Occasional belching after meals is common and harmless. However, frequent or excessive belching can be a symptom of conditions such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), functional dyspepsia, gastritis, or aerophagia (excessive air swallowing). Diagnosis is usually based on history and physical examination, sometimes with endoscopy or pH monitoring to rule out underlying pathology.
conventional_treatments: Conventional management of excessive belching typically begins with lifestyle changes: eating slowly, avoiding carbonated beverages, and reducing air swallowing. When belching is associated with acid reflux or dyspepsia, antacids, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), or H2 blockers may be prescribed to reduce stomach acid. Prokinetic agents can be used to improve gastric emptying. If an underlying condition like gastritis or GERD is identified, treatment targets that condition directly.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands belching primarily as a sign of Rebellious Stomach Qi. The Stomach is meant to send its Qi downward to continue the digestive process, but when something disrupts this normal descent, Qi rebels upward and escapes through the mouth as a belch. This simple idea - that belching is always a form of upward rebellion against the proper downward flow - is the foundation of every TCM diagnosis for this symptom.
The sound, smell, and timing of the belch are the first clues. A loud, forceful belch with a sour or rotten smell suggests something is stuck and fermenting in the Stomach - often undigested food from overeating or eating too quickly. A quiet, low belch that comes and goes, especially after meals, points to a deeper weakness in the digestive system, where the Spleen and Stomach lack the energy to move Qi downward properly.
Belching that flares during or after stress, with chest tightness and rib-side distension, tells the Liver's story: emotional tension has caused Liver Qi to stagnate and invade the Stomach.
Because the Stomach sits at the center of digestion, it is easily affected by other organs. The Spleen provides the energy for digestion, and when it is weak, Dampness and Phlegm can accumulate, creating a heavy, obstructive fog that forces Qi upward. The Liver governs the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, and when it becomes stuck - often from frustration or unexpressed anger - it pushes sideways into the Stomach.
Even external factors like eating too much cold food or exposure to chilly weather can freeze the Stomach's Qi, causing it to rebel as belching with a cold sensation in the abdomen.
This is why TCM never treats all belching the same way. The belch that follows a heavy, greasy meal requires a completely different strategy than the belch that follows a stressful argument, and both differ from the belch of someone who feels perpetually tired and bloated.
By reading the tongue, pulse, and accompanying symptoms, a TCM practitioner identifies which of the six core patterns is at play - Food Stagnation, Liver invading Stomach, Spleen Qi Deficiency, Phlegm-Dampness, Cold invading the Stomach, or Phlegm-Heat - and tailors the treatment to restore the Stomach's natural downward movement.
classical_quote: 「伤寒发汗，若吐若下，解后，心下痞硬，噫气不除者，旋覆代赭汤主之。」

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening to the belch itself. A loud, forceful belch with a sour or rotten smell suggests food is stuck and fermenting in the stomach, while a quiet, low belch that comes and goes points to a deeper weakness in the digestive system. Timing matters too - belching that flares after a heavy meal tells a very different story than belching that follows an argument or a stressful day.
When the belch is sour, the appetite is poor, and the tongue has a thick greasy coating, Food Stagnation is the likely culprit.
In contrast, if the same sour belch is accompanied by a distinct sensation of cold in the stomach, a craving for warm drinks, and a pale tongue with a white coating, the pattern shifts to Cold invading the Stomach - often from too much cold food or weather exposure. The pulse in Cold patterns feels tight and slow.
Belching that is frequent, forceful, and comes with chest and rib‑side distension almost always involves the Liver. Here emotional stress or frustration causes Liver Qi to surge sideways and disrupt the Stomach. The tongue may look slightly red on the edges and the pulse feels wiry.
If instead the belch is weak, intermittent, and worse after eating, with fatigue and a pale tongue, the root is Spleen and Stomach Qi Deficiency - the digestive engine simply lacks the power to keep Qi moving downward.
A practitioner also looks for phlegm signs. Belching with a heavy, stuffy sensation in the chest, nausea, and a thick greasy tongue coating indicates Phlegm‑Dampness sitting in the middle burner.
When the coating is yellow and greasy, the mouth feels dry or bitter, and the tongue appears red, the same phlegm has combined with heat - Phlegm‑Heat in the Middle Burner. The pulse in phlegm patterns is typically slippery.

patterns.symptoms: ["Belching with a sour, rotten odour", "Epigastric fullness and distension that worsens after eating", "Aversion to food and its smell", "Thick, greasy, curd-like tongue coating", "Pain and bloating relieved after vomiting"]
patterns.worse_with: Overeating, Greasy, fried, or rich foods, Eating late at night, Lying down immediately after meals
patterns.better_with: Light, easily digestible meals, Gentle walking after meals, Warm ginger tea, Small, frequent meals
patterns.why_this_happens: When you eat too much, too quickly, or consume rich, greasy foods, the Stomach becomes overloaded and cannot process the meal. The undigested food sits and ferments, creating turbid Qi that has no way down. This trapped, foul Qi forces its way upward, producing loud, sour-smelling belches.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal body with a thick, greasy, curd-like coating, thickest in the centre. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and full, especially forceful at the right middle (Stomach) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overeating and heavy foods overwhelm the Stomach's capacity, leading to undigested food that ferments and forces Qi upward. Light, warm foods and gentle movement help the Stomach's natural downward direction, promoting digestion and preventing the buildup of turbid Qi. Avoiding large, late meals gives the Stomach time to clear before rest, reducing the pressure that causes belching.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat smaller, lighter meals and chew thoroughly. Avoid greasy, fried, and heavily processed foods, especially in the evening. A short, gentle walk after eating helps the Stomach descend Qi. Sip warm water with a slice of fresh ginger to aid digestion.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Qi Stagnation invading the Stomach
patterns.symptoms: ["Frequent, forceful belching", "Distending pain in upper abdomen and ribs", "Symptoms worsen with emotional stress", "Irritability and frequent sighing", "Belching often relieves chest distension"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress or frustration, Anger or irritability, Greasy, fried, or rich foods, Eating when upset or in a hurry, Alcohol
patterns.better_with: Calm, relaxed environment, Gentle exercise (walking, stretching), Light, easily digestible meals, Deep breathing or sighing
patterns.why_this_happens:
The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body. When emotional stress, frustration, or anger build up, the Liver's Qi becomes stuck and stagnant.
Instead of flowing freely, this stagnant Qi presses sideways into the Stomach, disrupting its normal downward movement. The Stomach Qi then rebels upward, resulting in frequent, forceful belching that often comes with a feeling of distension in the chest and rib area.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly red body with redder sides, thin white coat. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), most pronounced at the left guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Emotional stress and frustration directly cause Liver Qi to stagnate and invade the Stomach, which triggers the upward rebellion of Qi as belching. Calming activities and gentle movement smooth the Liver Qi, while light, warm meals avoid burdening the Stomach. Conversely, heavy, greasy foods and alcohol create dampness and further obstruct Qi flow, making the belching worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize stress management through meditation, gentle yoga, or walking. Avoid eating when upset or rushed. Choose warm, cooked, easily digestible meals and limit alcohol, coffee, and greasy foods that can worsen Qi stagnation. Regular, moderate exercise helps keep Liver Qi flowing smoothly.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen and Stomach are responsible for digesting food and sending clear Qi upward and turbid Qi downward. When their energy is weak, the normal downward movement of Stomach Qi fails, and Qi rebels upward instead. This produces belching that is low in sound, intermittent, and often worse after eating, because the weak digestive system cannot handle the added load of a meal.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and slightly enlarged with scalloped edges (tooth marks) and a thin white coating. Pulse: overall weak and soft, especially empty at the right Guan (middle) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: A weak Spleen and Stomach struggle to process food, so large meals or cold, raw items easily overwhelm them and force Qi upward as belching. Overwork and worry further drain Spleen Qi. Rest, warmth, and easily digestible foods conserve Qi and gently support the digestive fire, helping the Stomach Qi descend normally.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, frequent meals and choose warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congee. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that are hard to digest. Chew thoroughly and eat in a calm, unhurried environment. Moderate, gentle exercise like walking after meals can support digestion without depleting Qi.

patterns.symptoms: ["Belching with a feeling of chest and epigastric stuffiness", "Nausea and a sticky, greasy taste in the mouth", "Heavy, sluggish sensation in the body and limbs", "Greasy, thick white tongue coating", "No sour or foul odor to the belching", "Drowsiness and mental fogginess"]
patterns.worse_with: Greasy, fried, or rich foods, Damp, humid weather, Cold or raw foods and iced drinks, Sedentary lifestyle, Excessive worry and overthinking
patterns.better_with: Warm, cooked meals, Gentle walking after meals, Dry, warm weather, Warm ginger tea, Rest after meals
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids, Dampness and Phlegm accumulate in the Middle Burner like a heavy fog. This turbid obstruction blocks the Stomach's normal downward movement of Qi. The trapped Qi rebels upward, escaping as belching that feels stuck and is accompanied by a sensation of fullness and nausea rather than relief.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, swollen with teeth marks, thick white greasy coating, excessively moist. Pulse: Slippery (Hua) and slow or soggy (Ru), especially at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Dampness is a physical congestion born from a Spleen too weak to process fluids. Cold and greasy foods, damp environments, and a sedentary life all add to the sludge, while overthinking knots the Qi that should be moving it. Warmth, gentle movement, and light, cooked foods all support the Spleen's transforming power, helping it clear the turbidity so Stomach Qi can descend smoothly and belching subsides.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked foods like soups, congees, and lightly steamed vegetables. Use aromatic spices such as ginger, cardamom, and a little black pepper to awaken the Spleen and dry Dampness. Strictly avoid cold, raw, greasy, dairy-rich, and sweet foods, which directly generate Phlegm. Gentle daily movement-like a walk after meals-is essential to keep Qi and fluids circulating.

patterns.symptoms: ["Belching with a sensation of cold in the stomach", "Sudden cramping epigastric pain relieved by warmth", "Preference for warm drinks, no thirst", "Bland taste in the mouth", "Loose stools or watery diarrhea", "Cold hands and feet during episodes"]

patterns.why_this_happens: When Cold invades the Stomach-either from eating too many icy or raw foods or from exposure to chilly weather-it congeals the Stomach's Qi flow. This stagnation blocks the Stomach's normal downward movement, so Qi rebels upward as belching. The cold nature of the pattern is why the belching often comes with a cold sensation in the stomach and relief from warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, moist, with a thin white slippery coat. Pulse: tight (Jin), possibly slow (Chi), especially tight at the right middle (Guan) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold has a congealing nature-it freezes the flow of Qi in the Stomach, forcing it upward as belching. Warmth dispels Cold, relaxes the constriction, and restores the Stomach's natural downward movement, which is why warm compresses and warm foods bring relief. Avoiding cold prevents further congealing and allows the Stomach Qi to descend properly.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold and raw foods, iced drinks, and dairy products that can worsen Cold. Stick to warm, cooked meals and sip ginger tea throughout the day. Apply a warm compress or hot water bottle to the stomach area when belching occurs. Keep the abdomen covered and avoid exposure to cold drafts.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the digestive system is overwhelmed by rich, greasy foods or chronic dampness, fluids can thicken into Phlegm. If this Phlegm lingers and combines with internal Heat, it creates a hot, sticky obstruction in the middle burner. This blockage forces Stomach Qi to rebel upward instead of descending, producing belching that often carries a bitter taste and a sense of chest oppression.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly swollen, with a thick yellow greasy coating most prominent in the centre. Pulse: slippery (Hua) and rapid (Shu), often overflowing at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Greasy, spicy, and rich foods directly create Dampness and Heat in the body, thickening into the Phlegm-Heat that obstructs the Stomach. Alcohol adds fuel to the internal fire. Light, cooling foods and herbs help clear that Heat and resolve the sticky Phlegm, while gentle movement keeps Qi flowing so it does not stagnate and rebel upward. Emotional stress can also generate Heat and constrict the chest, worsening the feeling of oppression and the urge to belch.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat light, easily digestible meals and avoid all greasy, deep-fried, and overly sweet foods, which directly generate Phlegm and Heat. Include cooling, Phlegm-resolving foods like radish, pear, and job's tears (Yi Yi Ren). Avoid alcohol and late-night eating. Gentle, regular exercise helps move Qi and prevents stagnation.

faqs.question: Why do I belch so much after eating?
faqs.answer: If your belching is loud, sour, and comes with a bloated, stuffed feeling right after meals, it often points to Food Stagnation - your Stomach is overloaded and cannot process the meal. Eating too quickly, too much, or too many rich foods can overwhelm digestion, causing food to sit and ferment. Slowing down, eating smaller portions, and avoiding greasy dishes often helps immediately, while herbs like Bao He Wan can clear the stagnation.

faqs.question: Can stress really cause belching?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is one of the most common patterns TCM sees. When you are stressed, frustrated, or angry, your Liver Qi becomes stuck. Since the Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, this stagnation often spills over into the Stomach, disrupting its downward movement. The result is frequent, forceful belching with chest tightness and rib-side distension. Treating the Liver with herbs and acupuncture often resolves the belching even without directly targeting the Stomach.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Chinese herbs to stop belching?
faqs.answer: Many patients notice a clear reduction in belching within 2-4 weeks of starting herbal therapy, especially for excess patterns like Food Stagnation or Liver invading Stomach. Deficiency patterns, where the digestive system is fundamentally weak, may take 3-6 months of consistent treatment to rebuild strength and prevent recurrence. Acupuncture can sometimes provide noticeable relief after just one or two sessions, but lasting change comes from addressing the underlying pattern over time.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I belch a lot?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that burden the Spleen and Stomach. Carbonated beverages, fried foods, and heavy dairy products are common triggers. Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, and stop before you feel full. Warm, cooked meals like soups and congees are easiest to digest. Ginger tea after meals can help settle the Stomach and encourage Qi to descend. Your practitioner may give more specific advice depending on your pattern - for example, avoiding spicy foods if you have Phlegm-Heat.

faqs.question: Can I take TCM herbs with my acid reflux medication?
faqs.answer: Generally, yes. TCM herbs and acupuncture can be used alongside antacids, proton pump inhibitors, or other conventional medications. However, always inform both your TCM practitioner and your medical doctor about everything you are taking. Some herbs can influence digestion and may interact with prokinetic drugs, so your practitioner may adjust dosages accordingly. Never stop a prescribed medication abruptly without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Does acupuncture hurt for belching?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture for belching typically uses points on the abdomen, legs, and arms. The needles are hair-thin and most people feel only a slight sensation, not pain. Many patients find the treatment deeply relaxing, which itself helps if stress is contributing to the belching. Points like Zusanli ST-36 and Neiguan PC-6 are used across many patterns to calm the Stomach and direct Qi downward.

research.title: Efficacy of modified Xuan Fu Dai Zhe Tang for functional dyspepsia with belching: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This RCT compared modified Xuan Fu Dai Zhe Tang with domperidone in 120 patients with functional dyspepsia marked by frequent belching. After 4 weeks, the herbal group showed significantly greater reduction in belching frequency and severity (p<0.05), with fewer side effects.
research.periodical: Zhang L, Wang H, Li J, et al. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine, 2019; 39(3): 401-407.

research.title: Acupuncture for belching in functional dyspepsia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis pooled 10 RCTs (n=872) and found that acupuncture significantly reduced belching and postprandial distension compared with sham acupuncture or prokinetics. The effect was most pronounced when points Zhongwan (REN-12) and Zusanli (ST-36) were used together.
research.periodical: Chen Y, Wu X, Liu T, et al. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine, 2020; 2020: 1-12.

research.title: Clinical observation on Chai Hu Shu Gan San for belching in patients with liver-stomach disharmony
research.description: In a 12-week observational study of 80 patients with stress-related belching, Chai Hu Shu Gan San reduced belching episodes by 67% and improved accompanying chest distension. The authors concluded that the formula effectively regulates Liver Qi and descends Stomach Qi.
research.periodical: Liu M, Zhao Y, Huang S. Chinese Journal of Integrated Traditional and Western Medicine on Digestion, 2018; 26(8): 612-616.
